transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: The Australian state of New South Wales has launched an ambitious program to protect its unique koala populations by creating 25,000 hectares of new koala habitat corridors over the next five years. The corridors will connect existing forest areas that have become fragmented by agriculture, urban development, and bushfires, allowing koalas to move safely between areas to find food, mates, and suitable living conditions. Koala populations in New South Wales have declined dramatically over the past 20 years, with estimates suggesting fewer than 30,000 koalas remain in the wild in the state following devastating bushfires in 2019 and 2020 that destroyed an estimated 25 percent of koala habitat. The program will involve planting over one million eucalyptus trees, the primary food source for koalas, as well as installing wildlife-friendly fencing and road crossings to reduce koala deaths from cars and dog attacks. The state government has committed 120 million Australian dollars to the initiative, with additional funding from environmental organizations and private donations. Conservationists have praised the program as an important step but say even more habitat protection will be needed to ensure koalas survive long-term. Koalas were listed as an endangered species in New South Wales and Queensland in 2022.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: A new study conducted by researchers at the University of Edinburgh has found that regularly playing board games and card games is associated with better cognitive function in adults over the age of 70. The study, which followed over 1,000 Scottish seniors for a period of three years, found that those who reported playing games like chess, bridge, Scrabble, or card games at least once a week scored significantly higher on tests of memory, problem-solving, and mental processing speed compared to non-players. Importantly, the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect cognitive health, including education level, physical activity, social interaction, and overall health, and still found a significant independent association between game playing and cognitive performance. The lead researcher suggested that board games provide multiple cognitive benefits simultaneously: they require memory, strategic thinking, concentration, and quick decision-making, and most are also social activities that reduce loneliness, which is itself a risk factor for cognitive decline. The study adds to a growing body of research suggesting that mentally stimulating leisure activities throughout life can help build "cognitive reserve" and may reduce the risk of developing dementia in old age. Researchers say the findings support expanding community game programs for seniors at libraries and senior centers.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What did the University of Edinburgh study find?
4. According to the researcher, why do board games provide cognitive benefits?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: A Norwegian company has begun operating the world's first zero-emission cargo ship, which entered service this month carrying containers between ports in Norway and Denmark. The vessel, named the Yara Birkeland, is powered entirely by electric batteries and autonomous navigation technology, producing no greenhouse gas emissions during operation. The ship can carry 120 shipping containers and will replace approximately 40,000 truck journeys per year along Norwegian coastal highways, reducing both road congestion and air pollution. While the ship will initially have a small crew on board for safety during a two-year testing period, the company plans to operate it fully autonomously by 2027, with all navigation, docking, and cargo monitoring controlled from an onshore operations center. The project has cost approximately 250 million Norwegian kroner, around 25 million US dollars, with the Norwegian government providing partial funding for the technology development. Maritime transport is responsible for nearly 3 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, and shipping companies are under increasing pressure from governments and environmental groups to reduce their climate impact. Several other major shipping companies are currently developing their own electric or hydrogen-powered vessels, though analysts say widespread adoption of zero-emission ships will take decades given the long lifespan of existing cargo vessels.

5. What is special about the Yara Birkeland?
6. How many truck journeys per year will the ship replace?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Chris): Hi Katie! Are you going to the careers fair on campus next Wednesday? I'm trying to decide if it's worth going, since I'm only a second-year student and I'm not graduating for another two years.

Woman (Katie): Oh, you should definitely go, Chris! I went last year when I was in my second year too, and it was actually really helpful even though I'm not looking for a job yet. I got to talk to representatives from so many different companies, and it helped me figure out what kinds of jobs I might actually be interested in once I graduate.

Man: Really? I was worried that all the companies would only want to talk to graduating students. I don't even know what field I want to go into yet. I'm studying business, but there are just so many different directions—marketing, finance, human resources, consulting. I feel overwhelmed.

Woman: That's exactly why you should go! Most companies love talking to second-years because they want to build relationships early for their internship programs. A lot of the big companies offer summer internships for students between their second and third years, and those internships often lead to full-time job offers later. I talked to a marketing agency last year, and they gave me really good advice about what classes I should take and what skills I should develop before applying.
Man: That sounds useful. What should I do to prepare? Should I bring copies of my resume? Mine's pretty bare right now, since I haven't had any real internships yet.

Woman: It doesn't matter if your resume is short—just bring a few copies anyway. It shows you're prepared. I'd also recommend looking at the list of companies attending on the careers website beforehand and picking out five or six that really interest you. That way you don't feel lost wandering around, and you can ask more specific questions. Ask them what a typical entry-level position looks like, what they look for in candidates, what the company culture is like.
Man: That makes sense. What should I wear? I don't want to show up in a suit if everyone else is in jeans.

Woman: Business casual is perfect—nice pants or khakis, a button-down shirt or a nice sweater, clean shoes. You don't need a full suit, but you don't want to look like you just rolled out of bed either. Also, bring a notebook so you can write down notes after talking to each company—after talking to ten different people, you'll forget who said what. And definitely ask for business cards or contact information if you have a good conversation with someone, so you can follow up with a thank-you email afterward.
Man: That's all really helpful advice, Katie. I think I'll go. Would you want to walk over together after our morning class?
Woman: Sure! I'm going again this year because there are a few companies I want to talk to about summer internships. We can compare notes afterward.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Megan): Hey Josh, do you have a minute? I need your advice about something. I'm thinking about getting a pet, but I can't decide between adopting a cat or a dog. I've never had a pet before as an adult, so I'm trying to figure out which would be better for my lifestyle.
Man (Josh): That's a big decision! Both are great, but they're really different in terms of time commitment and care. Let's start with your schedule. How much time do you usually spend at home?

Woman: I work full-time, about 40 hours a week, so I'm out of the house from around 8:30 to 6:00 most weekdays. I go to the gym two or three evenings after work, too. But I do work from home one day a week usually.

Man: Hmm, that's probably something to consider. Dogs are much more social and need a lot more attention. Most dogs don't do well being left alone for 9 or 10 hours a day regularly—they can get anxious or destructive. If you get a dog, you'd probably need to hire a dog walker to come midday, or take it to daycare a few times a week, which adds expense.

Woman: That's what I was worried about. I have friends who have dogs, and they seem to have to plan their whole lives around their pets—not being able to stay out late, needing to go home right after work to let the dog out. Cats seem more independent, right?

Man: Yeah, cats are definitely more self-sufficient. As long as you leave them enough food, water, and a clean litter box, they're perfectly fine being alone during the day. They're usually happy to see you when you get home, but they don't need constant attention. That said, they're not completely hands-off—they still need playtime, regular vet visits, and affection.
Woman: What about cost? I know dogs are generally more expensive, but how much more?

Man: Well, adoption fees are similar, but dogs eat more, you need to take them to training classes, grooming, more toys... and doggy daycare or walkers are a big added cost if you're out as much as you are. Vet bills for dogs can also be higher, especially for large breeds. Cats are usually cheaper overall, though vet bills can still add up.
Woman: Another thing is my apartment. It's not huge, about 700 square feet. Do you think that's too small for a dog?

Man: It depends on the dog. A big, active dog like a Labrador or a golden retriever would probably be miserable in a small apartment without a yard. But a smaller dog, like a Chihuahua or a French bulldog, might be okay if you take them for walks every morning and evening. Cats, though, do great in apartments—they don't need much space as long as they have a window to look out of and some vertical space to climb.

Woman: You're making a pretty strong case for a cat. I've always loved both, but I think a cat might fit my current lifestyle better. I can always adopt a dog later when I have a bigger place and more time.
Man: That makes sense. If you do get a cat, I'd recommend adopting two kittens together if you can—they keep each other company when you're out, and they're endlessly entertaining.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The invention of the microwave oven is a fascinating example of how accidental discoveries can lead to transformative everyday technologies. In 1945, an engineer named Percy Spencer was working for the Raytheon Corporation testing radar equipment when he noticed something strange: a chocolate bar he had in his pocket had melted while he was standing near an active magnetron, the vacuum tube that produces microwave signals for radar. Curious about this effect, Spencer began experimenting with other foods, starting with popcorn kernels, which popped when placed near the magnetron. He then tried heating an egg, which exploded when the inside cooked faster than the outside. Realizing the potential for cooking, Spencer and Raytheon developed the first commercial microwave oven, which was released in 1947. The original model, called the Radarange, was enormous—standing nearly 6 feet tall and weighing over 750 pounds—and cost the equivalent of tens of thousands of dollars in today's money, making it practical only for restaurants and commercial kitchens. It wasn't until the late 1960s that smaller, more affordable countertop models became available for home use, with prices dropping to under 200 dollars by the 1970s. Initial public reaction was mixed, with some people fearing that microwave radiation was dangerous or that food cooked in a microwave would be less nutritious. But as the technology proved safe and convenient, microwaves quickly became a standard appliance in American kitchens—today over 90 percent of US households own one. While the basic technology remains the same, modern microwaves include features like convection cooking, sensor reheating, and smart connectivity that Percy Spencer could never have imagined. Interestingly, the melting chocolate bar that started it all is now commemorated with a plaque at Raytheon's headquarters.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: The Lake District in northwest England is one of the most visited national parks in the United Kingdom, attracting over 18 million visitors annually. Famous for its stunning landscape of glacial lakes, rugged mountains, and picturesque stone villages, the region has inspired writers, artists, and nature lovers for centuries. The Lake District covers approximately 2,362 square kilometers and contains England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, which stands at 978 meters, as well as its deepest lake, Wastwater, which reaches a depth of 79 meters. The area's literary connections are particularly strong: the poet William Wordsworth lived in the Lake District for much of his life, and his poetry was deeply influenced by the region's natural beauty. He and fellow poets Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey became known as the "Lake Poets." Later, Beatrix Potter wrote many of her famous Peter Rabbit stories while living in the Lake District, and she left much of her property to the National Trust to help preserve the landscape. In 2017, the Lake District was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for both its natural beauty and its significant influence on the Romantic movement and on the development of modern ideas about landscape conservation. Tourism is the mainstay of the local economy, supporting thousands of jobs in hotels, restaurants, pubs, and outdoor activity centers. Visitors enjoy hiking, boating on the lakes, visiting historic houses, and sampling local foods such as Cumberland sausage and Grasmere gingerbread. While the large number of visitors brings economic benefits, it also creates challenges including traffic congestion, footpath erosion, and pressure on local housing prices as properties are bought as second homes.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: Imposter syndrome, the psychological pattern where people doubt their accomplishments and have a persistent fear of being exposed as a "fraud," is an extremely common experience, particularly among high-achieving individuals. Despite achieving external markers of success like good grades, promotions, or professional recognition, people experiencing imposter syndrome believe they are not as intelligent or competent as others perceive them to be, and often attribute their success to luck, timing, or simply being able to fool others. The concept was first identified in the 1970s by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, who initially studied the phenomenon in high-achieving women but later found that it affects people of all genders, ages, and professions. Research suggests that approximately 70 percent of people will experience imposter syndrome at some point in their lives, including many extremely accomplished individuals—famous examples include scientists Albert Einstein and Marie Curie, author Maya Angelou, and numerous CEOs and actors. Imposter syndrome can manifest in several ways: some people overwork to the point of burnout trying to prove they belong; some procrastinate out of fear they won't be able to do something perfectly; others downplay their achievements or avoid taking on new challenges because they don't believe they deserve success. The good news is that imposter syndrome can be managed. Experts recommend several strategies: talking about your feelings with trusted mentors or peers who can help you see your accomplishments more objectively; keeping a record of positive feedback and successes to refer to when self-doubt strikes; recognizing that no one is perfect and that even experts make mistakes and continue learning; and reframing your thoughts—instead of thinking "I don't know what I'm doing," try thinking "I'm still learning, and that's okay." Contrary to popular belief, imposter syndrome does not necessarily go away with experience; many people in senior positions still experience it, though they typically become better at managing those feelings over time.
